extracted.intended_audience: general readers and book-lovers seeking guidance on how to choose books, form reading habits, and how to travel for reflection
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and philosophical guidance on selecting what to read, ordering and systematising one's reading in an age of abundant printed matter, and related advice on solitary travel as a mode of contemplation. Focuses on cultivating taste, purpose, and balance in reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the habit of reading idly
rubrics_metrics.description: A habit of reading idly debilitates and corrupts the mind; 'reading for mere reading's sake' is one of the worst and commonest and most unwholesome habits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: frequent, purposeless consumption of trivial printed matter. Effect: weakens capacity for 'wholesome reading' and corrodes appreciation for substantial works. Remedy: cultivate deliberation and resolve to resist idle reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read with purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Every book taken up without a purpose is an opportunity lost of taking up a book with a purpose; stray information crammed in is likely to displace more important knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before reading, have a clear aim (education, moral improvement, specific knowledge). Prioritise books that serve that aim rather than casual or accidental reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strictly choose books because of limited time
rubrics_metrics.description: In the wilderness of books most men, certainly all busy men, must strictly choose; the vast multiplicity means we cannot read everything, so selection is necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat reading time as precious 'hours' to be allocated; prefer depth over breadth when time is short. Use selection rather than indiscriminate consumption to avoid being 'choked off' from the right books.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritise great books and masterpieces
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'good book' is 'an immortality rather than a life' — the truly vital books form a trifling portion of the whole and should be preferred to ephemeral literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure regular engagement with canonical works (Milton, Dante, Homer, Virgil, Shakespeare, etc.). Reserve the most precious reading time for works judged by long critical consent to be 'masterpieces.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance reading across types and aims
rubrics_metrics.description: A sound education should be comprehensive and symmetrical, appealing in turn to imagination, memory, and reflection — thus include poetry, history, science, and philosophy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid one-sided reading that focuses only on one genre or subject; aim for variety so no great type of thought is wholly a blank.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid parochial or narrow reading (one age/country/type)
rubrics_metrics.description: When reading exhausts itself in the literature of one age, one country, or one type, it tends to narrow or deform the mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include ancient writers and other national literatures; read across epochs and cultures to counteract parochialism and broaden perspective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Train and cultivate taste — appreciating great works is a learned faculty
rubrics_metrics.description: The reading of great books is a faculty to be acquired; an appetite for new, trivial works makes it hard to enjoy masterpieces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice sustained reading of demanding works; accept that enjoyment of classics may require a period of 'treatment' or training of the mind and nerves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematise and organise one's reading and knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: The first intellectual task of our age is rightly to order and make serviceable the vast realm of printed material — to organise our knowledge, to systematise our reading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop a scheme or plan of reading (a mini-curriculum or selection strategy) rather than ad hoc browsing; organise notes and priorities to prevent being overwhelmed by abundance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer books that teach, elevate, or inspire over mere entertainment
rubrics_metrics.description: To be simply entertained is to cease to be taught, elevated, inspired by books; mere gathering of chance information closes the mind to more urgent kinds of knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When choosing between readable/informative works and books that deepen moral or intellectual life, give precedence to the latter for limited reading time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resist novelty-for-novelty's-sake and conspicuous 'curiosities'
rubrics_metrics.description: People often choose 'something eccentric' because they never heard of it; printers and booksellers can make trivial gabble immortal and thereby tempt readers away from genuinely valuable works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be sceptical of works prized only for novelty or obscurity; use critical judgement to avoid being seduced by mere novelty or by printed 'curiosities.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Rely on long-established critical consensus for identifying the best works
rubrics_metrics.description: There are no secret 'tips' in literature; the world has long ago closed the great assize of letters and judged the first places everywhere — the judgment of the world is almost unerring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the canon and informed critical judgement as a guide to the 'best' authors rather than seeking esoteric recommendations or contrarian lesser lights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercise self-control in the face of mass printing
rubrics_metrics.description: Printing is a momentous boon but can be made a clog or curse if used unwisely; the multiplicity of printed matter entails responsibility and resolution to resist temptations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be deliberate about what to acquire and read; cultivate restraint against the flood of new publications and marketing that aim to attract attention rather than lasting value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim for reading that perfects the whole nature, not narrow curiosity
rubrics_metrics.description: A healthy mode of reading follows the lines of a sound education: its aims are comprehensive, not special; they give capacities rather than only materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select works that build intellectual capacities and moral character across different faculties, rather than simply accumulating interesting facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purge poor habits — undertake a course to restore taste
rubrics_metrics.description: The intellectual system of most of us needs 'to purge and to live cleanly' — only by a course of treatment shall we bring our minds to feel at peace with the grand pure works of the world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If current tastes are corrupted by ephemeral reading, deliberately withdraw from frivolous literature and practise reading classic works repeatedly to rebuild appreciation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognise that not all readable modern literature equals the masters
rubrics_metrics.description: Much modern literature may be readable and entertaining but does not replace the unique value of the masterpieces; we often read commentaries rather than the great works themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid substituting readable modern criticism, explanations, or lighter verse for direct engagement with canonical masterpieces; read originals when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer solitude on a journey for contemplation
rubrics_metrics.description: The author prefers to go by himself: 'I am then never less alone than when alone.' The soul of a journey is liberty to think, feel, and do as one pleases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When your goal is reflection or mental replenishment, travel alone so as to have uninterrupted breathing-space for reverie and inward thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not try to talk and think at the same time while travelling
rubrics_metrics.description: The writer cannot see the wit of walking and talking at the same time; to talk or to think well one must do one thing at a time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you want contemplative benefits from a journey, avoid conversational distraction; do not attempt sociable chatter when seeking inward experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the synthetical method on a journey — gather impressions first, analyse later
rubrics_metrics.description: On a journey the author prefers to 'lay in a stock of ideas then, and to examine and anatomise them afterwards' — he wants impressions to float before the breeze rather than immediate analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect sensory and associative impressions while travelling; defer analysis and argument until afterward to preserve the freshness of experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Either be entirely alone or fully sociable — avoid half-fellowship
rubrics_metrics.description: The author likes to be either entirely to himself, or entirely at the disposal of others; half-faced fellowship (partial company while musing) interferes with involuntary impressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose company deliberately for the journey's purpose: solitude for inwardness, or wholly sociable companionship for shared amusement; avoid ambiguous or intermittent company that frustrates both aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep some impressions private — do not force others to share or translate them
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a feeling in the air or a tone in the colour of a cloud which hits your fancy; to explain it for the benefit of others often ruins the impression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When moved by an impression while travelling, consider keeping it inward (a 'dumb show') rather than translating it into words and argument for companions; private brooding can be the proper end of travel.
